title: Git & GitHub
subtitle: First commit to rebase, reflog and pull requests

modules.title: What Git is, in one picture

lessons.title: What Git is, in one picture

blocks.text: Git saves snapshots of your project. Each snapshot is a **commit**. Git keeps every commit, so you can go back, compare, and work on several ideas side by side. GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your Git project so other people (and your other machines) can share it.
The four places your work can be. Most confusion in Git comes from not knowing which of these a command touches.
One-time setup

blocks.code:
git --version                          # check it is installed
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase true   # optional: keeps history straight when you pull

blocks.text: The loop you will repeat every day

blocks.code:
git status                 # where am I, what changed?
git diff                   # what exactly changed?
git add recipes/chai.txt   # choose what goes in the next snapshot
git commit -m "Add cardamom to chai"
git push                   # share it

blocks.text: Words you will hear

rows: A project folder that Git is tracking. The history lives in the hidden `.git` folder.
One saved snapshot, with a message, an author, and a unique ID (the hash, like `a1b2c3d`).
A movable name that points to a commit. Making a branch copies nothing; it just adds a name.
"You are here." Usually it points at the branch you are on.
Another copy of the repo, usually on GitHub. The default name is `origin`.
Download a full copy of a remote repo, including all history.
A GitHub page that says "please review my branch and merge it."
Two branches changed the same lines. Git stops and asks you to pick.

blocks.text: Every commit remembers its parent. That chain is the history. A branch is a label on one commit, and it moves forward each time you commit on it.
Try it: commit graph playground
Press the buttons and watch what each command does to the graph. Nothing here touches your real files. To type commands yourself, open the **Playground** tab.
Filled ring = the commit HEAD is on. A faded commit is no longer reachable from any branch; in real Git it still lives in the reflog for a while, which is how rescues work.
Branching commands

blocks.code:
git branch                    # list branches
git switch -c add-dosa        # create and move to a new branch
git switch main               # move back
git switch -                  # jump to the previous branch
git merge add-dosa            # bring add-dosa into the branch you are on
git branch -d add-dosa        # delete a merged branch

blocks.text: Both combine work. Merge keeps the true shape of history and adds one merge commit. Rebase replays your commits on top of the latest main, which gives a straight line but creates new commits with new IDs.
**Before.** feature started at B; main moved on to C.
**git merge feature.** New commit M joins both lines. Nothing is rewritten.
**git rebase main.** D and E are copied after C as D′ and E′. The old D and E are dropped.
**The one rule of rebase:** do not rebase commits that other people already pulled. Rebase your own unshared branch freely.
When two branches change the same line, Git writes both versions into the file between markers and stops.

blocks.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
- 1 tsp jaggery
=======
- half tsp sugar
>>>>>>> less-sugar

items: Run `git status` to see which files are in conflict.
Open each file, keep the lines you want, and delete the three marker lines.
`git add <file>` to mark it solved, then `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue` during a rebase).
Want out? `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` puts everything back.

blocks.text: Working with a remote

blocks.code:
git clone git@github.com:you/recipe-box.git   # download a repo
git remote -v                                  # see where origin points
git fetch                                      # download new commits, change nothing locally
git pull                                       # fetch + merge (or rebase) into your branch
git push -u origin add-dosa                    # first push of a new branch
git push                                       # later pushes

blocks.text: `git fetch` is always safe. If you are unsure what a pull will do, fetch first and look with `git log --oneline main..origin/main`.
Parking work: stash

blocks.code:
git stash push -m "wip peanuts"   # save uncommitted edits and clean the folder
git stash -u                      # also include brand-new files
git stash list
git stash pop                     # bring the latest one back

blocks.text: Marking releases: tags

blocks.code:
git tag -a v1.0 -m "First menu"
git push origin v1.0

blocks.text: Pick the undo by answering two questions: is it committed, and has anyone else seen it?
If the commit is already pushed, use `git revert`: it adds a new commit that cancels the old one, so nobody's history breaks. Lost something? `git reflog` lists every place HEAD has been.
What each reset mode touches

rows: You want to redo the last commit with the same changes.
You want to re-choose what to stage.
You want the commit and its changes gone.

blocks.text: `--hard` throws away uncommitted edits, and those cannot be recovered. Committed work can, through the reflog.
Everyday undo commands

blocks.code:
git restore chai.txt              # discard unstaged edits in one file
git restore --staged chai.txt     # unstage, keep the edits
git commit --amend                # fix the last message or add a forgotten file
git revert a1b2c3d                # new commit that cancels a1b2c3d (safe after push)
git restore --source=HEAD~3 chai.txt   # get an old version of one file
git clean -fdn                    # preview which untracked files would be deleted

blocks.text: The rescue: reflog

blocks.code:
git reflog                        # every move HEAD made, newest first
git reset --hard "HEAD@{1}"       # go back to where HEAD was one move ago
git switch -c rescued a1b2c3d     # or put a branch on a lost commit

blocks.text: Deleted a branch by mistake? Find its last commit in the reflog and run `git branch name <hash>`. Entries stay for about 90 days by default.
Finding the commit that broke something: bisect

blocks.code:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                    # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.0              # this old one worked
# Git checks out the middle commit. Test, then answer:
git bisect good    # or    git bisect bad
git bisect reset                  # when it names the culprit
git bisect run ./test.sh          # or let a script answer for you

blocks.text: Bisect halves the search each step, so 1,000 commits take about 10 checks.
Teams rarely push straight to `main`. You push a branch, open a pull request, checks run, someone reviews, and then it merges.
New pushes to the same branch update the open pull request. You never need to open a second one for fixes.
Connect your machine once (SSH)

blocks.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub      # paste into GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys
ssh -T git@github.com          # should greet you by username

blocks.text: Put the practice project on GitHub

blocks.code:
gh auth login                                  # GitHub CLI, once
gh repo create recipe-box --private --source=. --push
# without gh: create an empty repo on github.com, then
git remote add origin git@github.com:you/recipe-box.git
git push -u origin main

blocks.text: A pull request from the terminal

blocks.code:
git switch -c add-upma
# edit, add, commit
git push -u origin add-upma
gh pr create --fill            # title and body from your commits
gh pr status                   # checks and reviews
gh pr checkout 12              # try someone else's PR locally
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

blocks.text: Fork or branch?

rows: You have write access (your team's repo).

blocks.text: Three merge buttons

rows: All commits plus one merge commit
Keeping the full story of a long branch
One commit for the whole PR
Messy "fix typo" commits; most teams' default
Each commit replayed, no merge commit
Clean, meaningful commits you want to keep one by one

blocks.text: Automatic checks: GitHub Actions
Save this as `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It runs on every pull request.

blocks.code:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./run-tests.sh

blocks.text: Settings worth turning on

items: **Branch protection** on `main`: require a pull request, one approval, and passing checks.
**CODEOWNERS** file: the right reviewers are asked automatically.
**Pull request template** at `.github/pull_request_template.md`: what changed, how it was tested, screenshots.
**Secret scanning and push protection**: GitHub blocks pushes that contain known key formats.
Write `Closes #12` in the PR body and issue 12 closes when the PR merges.

modules.title: Using Git with AI coding tools

lessons.title: Using Git with AI coding tools

blocks.text: AI assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex) edit many files quickly. Git is what makes that safe: every AI change becomes a diff you can read, and one command takes it back.
Start clean, keep tasks small, and read the diff before anything is committed. If the result is wrong, discarding it costs nothing.

items: **Commit before you prompt.** A clean `git status` means the whole AI change is exactly `git diff`.
**One task, one branch.** Easy to review, easy to throw away.
**Stage in pieces** with `git add -p`. You approve each hunk, so nothing slips in unread.
**You approve the risky commands.** `push --force`, `reset --hard`, `clean -fd` and branch deletes should need your yes.
**Keep secrets out.** Put `.env` in `.gitignore` before the first commit, and check `git diff --staged` for keys.
**Say who wrote it.** Many teams add a `Co-Authored-By:` line to AI-assisted commits.

blocks.text: This Mac already follows the fourth habit: a hook in `~/ai-handoff/hooks` stops an AI session from running `git commit` unless you ask for it in that message.
Prompts that work well

rows: "Write a commit message: imperative subject under 60 characters, then why."
"Summarise what changed, why, and how to test it."
The conflicted file and both branch names
"Explain what each side intended, then propose a merged version. Do not pick one side silently."
"Why did these lines change over time?"
"Run `git bisect` with this test and tell me the first bad commit."
"Suggest how to squash these into logical commits. Show the plan first; do not run it."
"I did X and lost Y. What is the safest way back?"

blocks.text: Parallel AI sessions: worktrees
A worktree is a second folder on a different branch that shares the same repository. Two AI sessions can work at once without overwriting each other's files.

blocks.code:
git worktree add ../recipe-box-hotfix -b hotfix   # new folder, new branch
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../recipe-box-hotfix          # when the branch is merged
claude --worktree add-upma                        # Claude Code: start a session in its own worktree

blocks.text: AI on GitHub itself

items: **Claude Code** can run the whole loop when you ask in words: "commit this", "open a PR". It uses your `git` and `gh`.
**@claude on pull requests:** run `/install-github-app` in Claude Code to add the GitHub Action, then mention `@claude` in a PR or issue comment to ask for a review or a fix.
**Copilot and Cursor** have a button that drafts a commit message from the staged diff. Read it; it describes what changed, and you often need to add why.
**AI review is a first pass.** A person still approves the merge.

blocks.text: Tell the AI your Git rules
Put the rules in the file your tool reads at the start of each session (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, or Cursor rules).

blocks.code:
# Git rules for this repo
- Never commit or push unless I ask.
- Branch names: feature/<ticket>-short-name
- Commit subject: imperative, under 60 characters.
- Never force-push, never rewrite main.
- Do not touch generated files or .env.

git config --global alias.st  "status -sb"
git config --global alias.lg  "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
git config --global alias.last "log -1 --stat"
git config --global alias.undo "reset --soft HEAD~1"
git config --global alias.amend "commit --amend --no-edit"

blocks.text: Fourteen short labs on one tiny project. Type them yourself in an empty folder, or run the script to build the finished repo and read its history.

The script was last run on 12 Nov 2026 with Git 2.50.1 and all 14 labs behaved as described below. The finished repo is at `~/Documents/git-practice-recipe-box`. To start again, delete that folder and re-run, or pass another folder name to the script.

modules.title: What you need, and a four-week plan

rows: Pull requests from the terminal; AI tools use it too
An editor with a diff view

blocks.text: Where to spend your study time
A suggested split of about 20 hours. This is a recommendation for a beginner, not measured data.
Daily basics and branching take more than half the time because every later skill depends on them.

lessons.title: Four weeks, about an hour a day

blocks.text: Start here + labs 1 to 3. Goal: commit without thinking, read `git status` and `git diff`, write a `.gitignore`.
Core Git + labs 4 to 7. Goal: branch, merge, solve one conflict by hand, rebase a branch, use stash.
Undo & rescue + labs 8 to 13. Goal: choose the right undo from the flowchart, recover a commit with reflog, run one bisect.
GitHub + Git with AI + lab 14. Goal: push the project, open and merge a pull request, add one Action, do one AI-assisted change through the safe loop. Then read the interview questions.

questions.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
questions.a: Git is the version control tool that runs on your machine and records history. GitHub is a hosting service for Git repositories that adds pull requests, issues, code review and automation. You can use Git with no GitHub at all.

questions.q: What are the three states a file can be in?
questions.a: Modified (changed in the working folder), staged (marked for the next commit) and committed (saved in the repository). A fourth practical state is untracked: a new file Git has never been told about.

questions.q: Why does Git have a staging area?
questions.a: It lets you choose exactly what goes into a commit. You can change five files and commit two of them, or even part of one file with git add -p, so each commit is one logical change.

questions.q: What is a commit, internally?
questions.a: A snapshot of the whole tracked tree plus metadata: author, date, message and the ID of its parent commit(s). Its hash is computed from all of that, so changing anything gives a different commit.

questions.q: What is HEAD?
questions.a: A pointer to what you have checked out. Normally it points to a branch name, and that branch points to a commit. If HEAD points straight at a commit, you are in "detached HEAD".

questions.q: git fetch versus git pull?
questions.a: fetch downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main, without touching your branch or files. pull is fetch followed by a merge or rebase into your current branch.

questions.q: What does git clone do?
questions.a: Copies the entire repository with all history, sets up a remote called origin, creates remote-tracking branches and checks out the default branch.

questions.q: What is .gitignore, and how do you stop tracking a file already committed?
questions.a: A list of path patterns Git should not track. It has no effect on files already tracked; for those run git rm --cached , commit, and add the pattern.

questions.q: How do you write a good commit message?
questions.a: A short imperative subject of about 50 to 60 characters ("Add cardamom to chai"), a blank line, then a body that explains why the change was needed. The diff already shows what changed.

questions.q: What is a branch?
questions.a: A lightweight movable pointer to a commit, stored as a small file containing one hash. Creating one is instant and copies no files.

questions.q: Merge versus rebase?
questions.a: Merge joins two histories with a merge commit and preserves what really happened. Rebase replays your commits on a new base, giving linear history but new commit IDs. Rebase private branches; merge shared ones.

questions.q: What is a fast-forward merge?
questions.a: If the target branch has no new commits since the feature branched off, Git just moves the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is made. Use --no-ff to force one.

questions.q: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
questions.a: git status lists conflicted files. Edit each file to the correct content and remove the markers, git add it, then git commit (or git rebase --continue). git merge --abort backs out.

questions.q: git reset versus git revert?
questions.a: reset moves the branch pointer backward and so rewrites history; use it on unpushed commits. revert makes a new commit that undoes an earlier one; use it on shared history.

questions.q: Explain reset --soft, --mixed and --hard.
questions.a: All three move the branch pointer. soft keeps the staging area and files. mixed (the default) clears staging but keeps files. hard also overwrites the working files.

questions.q: git restore versus git reset versus git checkout?
questions.a: restore changes files in the working folder or staging area. reset moves the branch pointer. checkout used to do both jobs plus switching branches; switch and restore were added to split it up.

questions.q: What is git stash and when would you use it?
questions.a: It saves uncommitted changes on a stack and cleans the working folder. Use it to switch branches quickly or pull without committing half-done work. stash pop brings it back.

questions.q: What is a detached HEAD and how do you get out?
questions.a: HEAD points at a commit instead of a branch, for example after checking out a tag. Commits made there belong to no branch. Keep them with git switch -c new-name, or leave with git switch main.

questions.q: What is cherry-pick?
questions.a: It applies the change from one specific commit onto your current branch as a new commit. Typical use: copying a bug fix to a release branch.

questions.q: What does git commit --amend do, and when is it unsafe?
questions.a: It replaces the last commit with a new one containing the updated message or staged changes. It is unsafe after the commit has been pushed and pulled by others, because the old commit ID disappears.

questions.q: What are origin and upstream?
questions.a: Conventional remote names. origin is where you cloned from. In a fork workflow, origin is your fork and upstream is the original project.

questions.q: What is a remote-tracking branch?
questions.a: A local read-only record such as origin/main that shows where the remote branch was at your last fetch. Your local main "tracks" it, which is how git status can say you are 2 commits ahead.

questions.q: What is the difference between a lightweight and an annotated tag?
questions.a: A lightweight tag is just a name on a commit. An annotated tag is its own object with tagger, date and message, and can be signed. Use annotated tags for releases.

questions.q: How do you squash several commits into one?
questions.a: git rebase -i HEAD~3 and mark the later commits as squash or fixup. Or git reset --soft HEAD~3 followed by one new commit. On GitHub, "Squash and merge" does it at merge time.

questions.q: What does git diff show with no arguments, with --staged, and with HEAD?
questions.a: No arguments: working folder versus staging. --staged: staging versus the last commit. HEAD: working folder versus the last commit, staged or not.

questions.q: What is the reflog and how does it save you?
questions.a: A local log of every position HEAD and each branch has had. After a bad reset, rebase or branch delete, find the old commit ID there and reset or branch to it. It is local only and expires (90 days by default).

questions.q: How does git bisect work?
questions.a: Binary search over history. You mark one good and one bad commit; Git checks out the midpoint and you say good or bad until it isolates the first bad commit. With bisect run, a script answers.

questions.q: What are the four Git object types?
questions.a: Blob (file content), tree (a folder listing: names pointing to blobs and trees), commit (points to a tree and to parent commits) and annotated tag. All are stored by the hash of their content.

questions.q: Why is --force-with-lease safer than --force?
questions.a: It only overwrites the remote branch if it is still where your last fetch saw it. If a teammate pushed in between, the push is rejected instead of destroying their commits.

questions.q: What is interactive rebase used for?
questions.a: Editing your own unpushed history: reorder, squash, reword, edit or drop commits. git rebase -i main opens the list of commits to change.

questions.q: What are Git hooks?
questions.a: Scripts in .git/hooks that run at events such as pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push. Used for linting, message checks and blocking secrets. They are not cloned, so teams share them through a tool or core.hooksPath.

questions.q: What is a worktree?
questions.a: An extra working folder attached to the same repository, checked out on a different branch. It lets you fix a bug on one branch while a build or an AI session runs on another, with no stashing.

questions.q: Submodule versus subtree?
questions.a: A submodule stores a pointer to a specific commit of another repository; contributors must init and update it. A subtree copies the other project's files into your repo, which is simpler for consumers but makes pushing changes back harder.

questions.q: What do git gc and packfiles do?
questions.a: Git first stores each object as a separate compressed file. gc packs them into packfiles using delta compression and removes unreachable objects past their expiry, which keeps the repo small and fast.

questions.q: What is rerere?
questions.a: "Reuse recorded resolution." When enabled, Git records how you solved a conflict and applies the same solution automatically if the identical conflict appears again, for example during repeated rebases.

questions.q: Shallow clone versus partial clone?
questions.a: A shallow clone (--depth 1) cuts off history. A partial clone (--filter=blob:none) keeps all commits but downloads file contents only when needed. Both speed up CI on large repos.

questions.q: What is Git LFS?
questions.a: Large File Storage replaces big binary files with small pointer files in the repo and keeps the real content on a separate server, so clones stay small.

questions.q: How do signed commits work?
questions.a: You sign commits with a GPG or SSH key (git commit -S). GitHub checks the signature against keys on your account and shows "Verified". It proves the commit came from the key holder.

questions.q: You committed to main by mistake instead of a feature branch. Fix it.
questions.a: If not pushed: git branch feature (keeps the commits), git reset --hard origin/main (moves main back), git switch feature. If already pushed to a shared main, revert instead.

questions.q: You pushed a secret key. What now?
questions.a: Revoke and rotate the key first; assume it is compromised. Then remove it from history with git filter-repo or BFG, force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone. Removing it in a new commit is not enough.

questions.q: Your branch is far behind main and the PR shows conflicts. What do you do?
questions.a: git fetch, then git rebase origin/main (or merge origin/main if the branch is shared). Resolve conflicts commit by commit, run tests, and push with --force-with-lease if you rebased.

questions.q: A release is broken and you do not know which commit did it.
questions.a: Find the last good tag, run git bisect start , and use bisect run with a test that reproduces the bug. Revert the offending commit, then fix it properly on a branch.

questions.q: You ran git reset --hard and lost two commits.
questions.a: git reflog, find the entry before the reset, then git reset --hard that hash. If the work was never committed, Git cannot bring it back; check your editor's local history.

questions.q: How would you set up a branching strategy for a small team?
questions.a: Trunk-based: short-lived feature branches off main, pull requests with required review and CI, squash merges, release tags. Add release branches only if you must support old versions.

questions.q: Describe a pull request you would approve quickly.
questions.a: Small and single-purpose, with a description of what and why, tests or test notes, passing CI, and no unrelated formatting changes.

questions.q: Fork versus clone?
questions.a: A fork is your own server-side copy of someone else's repository on GitHub. A clone is a local copy on your machine. For open source you fork, clone your fork, and open a PR back to the original.

questions.q: What is branch protection?
questions.a: Rules on a branch such as main: require pull requests, approvals, passing status checks and up-to-date branches, and block force-pushes and deletion.

questions.q: What is GitHub Actions?
questions.a: GitHub's built-in automation. YAML workflows in .github/workflows run jobs on events like push or pull_request: tests, builds, deployments.

questions.q: Squash merge, merge commit, or rebase merge on GitHub?
questions.a: Squash turns the PR into one commit, good for tidy history. Merge commit preserves every commit and the branch shape. Rebase merge replays commits without a merge commit. Teams usually pick one and enforce it.

questions.q: What is a CODEOWNERS file?
questions.a: A file mapping paths to people or teams. GitHub requests their review automatically when those paths change, and branch protection can require their approval.

questions.q: How do you use Git safely with an AI coding assistant?
questions.a: Start from a clean tree on a new branch, give small tasks, read git diff before staging, stage with git add -p, run tests, and keep destructive commands behind your approval. Every AI change is then reviewable and reversible.

questions.q: Why are worktrees useful with AI agents?
questions.a: Each agent gets its own folder and branch on the same repository, so several can work in parallel without overwriting each other's uncommitted files. Each result arrives as a separate branch to review.

questions.q: Should AI-written code go through a pull request?
questions.a: Yes, the same as human code: CI, a human reviewer and a clear description. Many teams also mark it with a Co-Authored-By trailer so the history shows where AI was involved.

questions.q: How can an AI help resolve a merge conflict responsibly?
questions.a: Give it the conflicted file and the intent of both branches, ask it to explain each side before proposing a result, then review the merged file and run tests yourself. It should never silently drop one side.
